name: The Two Truths
desc:
[[conventional|conventional truth]] and [[ultimate|ultimate truth]]. Their function is neither to destroy worldly causality nor to cling to any ultimate substantial reality, thereby avoiding at once the two extremes of eternalism and annihilationism.

“Truth” (satya) means “real”, but the two truths are “real” in different ways: conventional truth is “real for the world” — because the world is inverted, illusory dharmas arise, and these dharmas are real for the world; ultimate truth is “real for the noble ones” — because the noble ones truly know the nature of inversion, they know that all dharmas are empty and unborn. The two truths are therefore not two worlds but two levels of cognition with respect to one and the same set of dharmas.

Interpretations differ considerably among the schools:
- Sarvāstivāda: distinguishes “dharmas” (substantially real) from “provisional designations” (prajñapti-sat);
- Madhyamaka: the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* (Zhong lun), “Examination of the Four Noble Truths”: “The Buddhas teach the Dharma in reliance on the two truths: one the conventional truth, the other the ultimate truth” — the two truths belong to the level of verbal teaching, and the Sanlun school goes further, using “the truth for [the world] / the truth as teaching” to state explicitly that the two truths “are only a teaching device, and have nothing to do with the object or the principle”;
- Yogācāra: the conventional is what consciousness manifests, the ultimate is suchness revealed by the two emptinesses.

The practical significance of the two truths is this: without destroying the conventional one realises the ultimate, and so one can observe the precepts, practise, and bear ethical responsibility, while clinging to no single dharma as ultimate.

src.t: *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* (Zhong lun), fascicle 4, “Examination of the Four Noble Truths”
src.q: “The Buddhas teach the Dharma to sentient beings in reliance on [[two_truths|the two truths]]: one is the conventional truth, the other the ultimate truth. Those who cannot understand this distinction between the two truths do not know the true meaning of the profound Buddha-Dharma.”

src.t: *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* (Zhong lun), fascicle 4, “Examination of the Four Noble Truths”
src.q: “Without relying on the conventional truth, the ultimate truth is not attained; not attaining the ultimate truth, [[nirvana|nirvāṇa]] is not attained.”
“The Buddhas' teaching always relies on the conventional truth and the ultimate truth; both are true, and it is no falsehood.”
“In the Buddha-Dharma there are [[two_truths|two truths]]: one is the conventional truth, the other the ultimate truth.”

tt.form: c. 5th century BCE (the distinction between conventional and ultimate)
tt.fix: The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* (Nāgārjuna, c. 150–250) established the two truths as levels of teaching; Jizang's *Er Di Yi* (Meaning of the Two Truths) and *Da Cheng Xuan Lun* (Profound Treatise on the Mahāyāna) set up “the two truths as verbal teaching” (6th–7th century); Yogācāra additionally established four levels of conventional and ultimate (7th century)
tt.trans: Translated by Kumārajīva under the Yao Qin (Later Qin): *Zhong lun* (c. 401–409); the *Da Zhidu Lun* likewise issued from Kumārajīva's translation bureau

name: Conventional Truth
desc:
The truth agreed upon by the world. Causality, good and evil, practice, and liberation all hold at this level.

“Conventional” (saṃvṛti) has the two senses of “covering, concealing” and “common consent, convention”: first, the cognition of ordinary beings is covered by [[ignorance|ignorance]]; second, the world takes linguistic convention as real. Conventional truth is therefore “valid but not ultimate”: within the conventional truth, killing is evil, giving is good, and causality is not deceptive; yet none of this holds as intrinsic existence.

[[madhyamaka|Madhyamaka]] stresses “not destroying the conventional”: precisely because without the conventional truth “the ultimate truth is not attained” — the ultimate cannot be found elsewhere, apart from the language and causality of the conventional.

src.t: *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* (Zhong lun), fascicle 4, “Examination of the Four Noble Truths”
src.q: In Piṅgala's commentary (Qingmu shi): “[[conventional|Conventional truth]] means that all dharmas are empty by nature, yet because the world is inverted, illusory dharmas arise, and these are real for the world.”

tt.fix: The definition given in Piṅgala's commentary on the *Zhong lun*

rel.dependent_origination: the level at which causality holds

name: Ultimate Truth
desc:
The ultimate truth: all dharmas are empty, without intrinsic nature, ungraspable.

“Ultimate” (paramārtha) is “the most excellent object of meaning”, referring to the object of the noble ones' wisdom. Its content is not “another, more real entity” but the fact itself that “all dharmas are without intrinsic nature”.

Ultimate truth therefore cannot be expressed positively — whatever is spoken is already conventional speech. This is why the *[[doc_29|Mūlamadhyamakakārikā]]* (Zhong lun) uses the “eight negations” in a via negativa, and it is also where the apparent tension lies between “the real mark cannot be spoken” and “the three baskets and twelve divisions” (the latter being precisely the necessary expedient of pointing at the moon with words).

src.t: *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* (Zhong lun), fascicle 4, “Examination of the Four Noble Truths”
src.q: In Piṅgala's commentary: “Because the noble sages truly know the nature of inversion, they know that all dharmas are empty and unborn; for the noble ones this is the ultimate truth, and it is called real.”

name: Emptiness
desc:
The meaning of being without intrinsic nature, and not “nothing exists”. What “emptiness” negates is only one thing: intrinsic nature (svabhāva) — a mode of existence that is not dependent on anything else, does not change, and stands independently.

The expression of emptiness is usually given in dependence on [[dependent_origination|dependent origination]]. The famous verse of the *[[doc_29|Mūlamadhyamakakārikā]]* (Zhong lun), “Examination of the Four Noble Truths”, runs: “Whatever is dependently originated, that I call emptiness; it is also a provisional designation, and it is also called the meaning of the middle way.” The three phrases correspond respectively to: because it is dependently originated it is without intrinsic nature (emptiness); being without intrinsic nature it is provisionally designated (provisional); it falls into neither of the two extremes of existence and non-existence (middle). Emptiness, the provisional, and the middle are therefore not three stages but three facets of one and the same statement — and this too became the classical basis of the Tiantai doctrine of the three truths.

The relation between emptiness and non-self is direct: emptiness is non-self, and non-self is emptiness. The two refer to the same thing; only “emptiness” lays stress on the level of dharmas, while “non-self” lays stress on the level of persons.

src.t: *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* (Zhong lun), fascicle 4, “Examination of the Four Noble Truths”
src.q: “Whatever is dependently co-arisen, that I call emptiness; it is also a provisional designation, and it is also called the meaning of the middle way.”

src.t: *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra* (Heart Sutra, Bore Boluomiduo Xin Jing)
src.q: “Form is emptiness, emptiness is form; feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are likewise so.”
A detailed exposition of the meaning of emptiness, distinguishing “the emptiness of sentient beings” from “the emptiness of dharmas”.

tt.form: c. 1st century BCE – 2nd century CE (the emergence of the Prajñāpāramitā sūtras)
tt.fix: Systematised in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* (Nāgārjuna, c. 150–250); for the Chinese *Heart Sutra* the Xuanzang version (649) is the most widely used
tt.trans: Chinese translations of the Prajñāpāramitā scriptures: Lokakṣema, *Daoxing Banruo Jing* (Daoxing Prajñā Sūtra), Eastern Han (179); Kumārajīva, *Dapin Banruo Jing* (Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā), Yao Qin (404); Xuanzang, *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in six hundred fascicles, Tang (660–663)

rel.anatta: emptiness is non-self, non-self is emptiness

name: The Three Doors of Liberation
desc:
Emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness (also rendered as non-activity, wu zuo). These are three contemplative doors entering into liberation, closely related to the [[two_truths|two truths]] and the [[three_natures|three natures]].

- The door of emptiness: contemplating all dharmas as without self and without anything belonging to a self, all dharmas being illusory and unreal;
- The door of signlessness: because of emptiness, not attaching to signs, free from all signs;
- The door of wishlessness: because of signlessness, having no craving or aspiration with respect to birth-and-death in the three realms.

The treatises make two key distinctions. First, the “three samādhis” extend to both defiled and undefiled, whereas the “three doors of liberation” are exclusively undefiled — *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (Jushe lun), fascicle 28: “Each of these three is of two kinds, pure and undefiled … among them the undefiled ones are called the three doors of liberation, because they can serve as the entrance to nirvāṇa.” Second, the Yogācāra school establishes the three doors by way of the three natures — *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Yoga Shidi Lun), fascicle 74, establishes the door of liberation of emptiness by the imagined nature, the door of liberation of wishlessness by the dependent nature, and the door of liberation of signlessness by the perfected nature.

*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Da Zhidu Lun), fascicle 20, uses the image that “the city of nirvāṇa has three gates”, and says: “These three doors of liberation are one dharma in the Mahāyāna; because of the cause of practice they are spoken of as three kinds” — the three doors are in fact one dharma, opened into three according to the differing faculties of sentient beings (those with much craving, those with much view, those with craving and view equally).

As to provenance it should be noted that the name “three doors of liberation” does not occur in the four Pali Nikāyas; it is a later fixed formulation. It occurs in Dharmarakṣa's translation *Fo Shuo Lishi Yi Shan Jing*, in Saṅghadeva's translation of the *Ekottara-āgama* (Zeng Yi Ahan), sūtra 8.3, and in Dānapāla's *Fo Shuo Fayin Jing*, and corresponds to sūtra 80 of the *Saṃyukta-āgama* (Za Ahan Jing) and to the *Fo Shuo Sheng Fayin Jing* — the latter being precisely the possible source of the name “three seals of the Dharma”.

src.q: Through the three contemplations of emptiness, signlessness, and nothingness, one finally contemplates [[anatta|non-self]] and nothing belonging to a self, thereby abandoning the habit of conceit and attaining purity of knowledge and vision; this is called the “seal of the noble Dharma”.
“Among them the undefiled ones are called the [[three_doors|three doors of liberation]], because they can serve as the entrance to nirvāṇa.”

“The real mark of all dharmas is the city of [[nirvana|nirvāṇa]], and the city has three gates: emptiness, signlessness, and non-activity.” “In the Mahāyāna it is one dharma; because of the cause of practice it is spoken of as three kinds.”
“The three doors of liberation are likewise established by way of the three natures.”

tt.form: c. 5th century BCE (the contemplative method of the three samādhis)
tt.fix: The name “three doors of liberation” is not found in the four Pali Nikāyas and is a later fixed formulation (c. 1st–4th century); its correlation with the three natures appears in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (4th–5th century)

rel.three_natures: established by way of the three natures

name: The Three Natures
desc:
The structure of delusion and awakening in [[vijnapti_matra|consciousness-only]] (Yogācāra): the [[parikalpita|imagined nature]], the dependent nature, and the perfected nature. The three are not three worlds but three cognitive states with respect to one and the same dependently originated dharma.

Their relation is as follows:
- The dependent nature — all dharmas arise from causes and conditions and appear in dependence on consciousness; this is the actual level of existence;
- The imagined nature — falsely grasping the dharmas of the dependent nature as possessing independent intrinsic nature; this belongs to “delusion”;
- The perfected nature — on the basis of the dependent nature, being free from the imagined nature and realising the suchness revealed by the two emptinesses; this belongs to “awakening”.

Hence within the three natures the dependent nature is the pivot: neither delusion nor awakening is apart from it, the difference lying only in whether grasping has arisen upon it. The correspondence with the two truths is: the imagined nature is provisional existence, the dependent nature is conventional existence, the perfected nature is ultimate existence.

The three natures are also the basis on which the three doors of liberation are established (see *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 74); this group of concepts therefore runs through Yogācāra ontology, epistemology, and soteriology at once.

src.t: *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* (Jie Shenmi Jing), “Chapter on the Marks of All Dharmas” (Yi Qie Fa Xiang Pin)
src.q: It establishes the three marks as “the mark of the imagined nature, the mark of the dependent nature, and the mark of the [[chengshi|perfected]] nature”; this is the scriptural source of the doctrine.

src.t: *Cheng Weishi Lun* (Discourse on the Perfection of Consciousness-only), fascicles 8 and 9
src.q: A systematic exposition of the [[three_natures|three natures]] and their correlation with the two truths.
The three doors of liberation are established by way of the [[three_natures|three natures]].

tt.fix: *Cheng Weishi Lun* (compiled and translated by Xuanzang, 659)
tt.trans: Tang: Xuanzang's translation of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* (647); the *Cheng Weishi Lun* (659)

rel.vijnapti_matra: establishes, by way of the three natures, that consciousness exists and its objects do not

name: The Imagined Nature
desc:
Falsely grasping the dharmas of the dependent nature as possessing independent intrinsic nature; this is the side of “delusion”. “Imagining” (parikalpa) means “conceiving everywhere” — the mind measures and grasps universally with respect to all dharmas, taking them as existent with intrinsic nature.

Its characteristic is “affirmed in sentient experience but absent in reality” (qing you li wu): it genuinely exists in the cognition of sentient beings (affirmed in sentient experience), but it does not exist in the actual dharmas (non-existent in principle). It is therefore not “yet another thing” but “an error”.

This distinction is the key to how [[vijnapti_matra|consciousness-only]] deals with “delusion”: delusion is not an extra layer of world, but a misreading of the world that is already there.

src.q: “The imagined nature is affirmed in sentient experience but absent in reality.”

src.t: *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* (Jie Shenmi Jing), “Chapter on the Marks of All Dharmas” (Yi Qie Fa Xiang Pin)
src.q: The definition of the mark of the imagined nature.

name: The Dependent Nature
desc:
All dharmas arise from causes and conditions and appear in dependence on consciousness; this belongs to the level of [[dependent_origination|dependent origination]]. “Dependent on others” (paratantra) means “arising in dependence on other conditions” — not autonomous, not independent, entirely constituted by conditions.

The dependent nature is the pivot among the [[three_natures|three natures]] and also the focus of the most concentrated discussion between Yogācāra and Madhyamaka: Madhyamaka holds that the dependent nature is synonymous with dependent origination, that is, “without intrinsic nature”; Yogācāra, by contrast, diverges from Madhyamaka in acknowledging the dependent nature as “truly existent” (the dependent nature exists; it is only that the imagined nature does not exist upon it).

Within the Yogācāra system the dependent nature corresponds directly to “consciousness” — since it appears in dependence on consciousness, the dependent nature is what consciousness transforms.

src.q: “The dependent nature is real in principle but non-existent in deluded sentient experience” — the dependent nature has its own distinct substantiality, unlike the imagined nature, which is wholly non-existent.
It takes the dependent nature as “the nature of discrimination” (vikalpa-svabhāva).

name: The Perfected Nature
desc:
Being free from the imagined nature on the basis of the dependent nature, and realising the [[suchness|suchness]] revealed by the two emptinesses (the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of dharmas); this is the side of “awakening”.

“Consummate” means complete, “accomplished” means achieved, “real” means true. It is not a new thing that needs to be produced, but the actual state revealed on the dependent nature once false grasping has been removed. The practice of [[vijnapti_matra|consciousness-only]] is therefore not “acquisition” but “turning away and turning toward” (zhuan she zhuan de) — what is discarded is the imagined nature, what is obtained is the perfected nature.

The perfected nature is suchness, namely the unconditioned of suchness among the six unconditioned dharmas, and it is the ultimate truth of consciousness-only.

src.t: *Cheng Weishi Lun* (Discourse on the Perfection of Consciousness-only), fascicles 8 and 9
src.q: “The real nature of all dharmas, consummate and accomplished, revealed by the two emptinesses, is called the [[chengshi|perfected]] nature.”

name: The Eight Consciousnesses
desc:
Eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mind-consciousness, manas, and [[alaya|ālaya-consciousness]]. The first six consciousnesses discern coarse objects, manas constantly examines and deliberates, and ālaya-consciousness retains the seeds and receives perfuming.

How the doctrine of the eight consciousnesses came to be established: the first five consciousnesses are sensory cognition; the sixth, mind-consciousness, synthesises and discerns, and also takes past and future as its objects; the seventh, manas, constantly and persistently considers the eighth consciousness as “I”, and is the direct source of self-grasping; the eighth, ālaya, contains all seeds, becomes manifest when conditions obtain, and performs the function of being the vehicle of the [[continuity|continuity]] of karma.

The significance of this system lies in solving the technical problem of “rebirth without a self”: there is no need to posit a substantial soul, yet one must explain how karma continues across lives — ālaya-consciousness performs precisely this function by way of “the continuity of consciousness” rather than “the transmigration of a substance”.

src.t: *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, “Chapter on the Marks of Mind, Manas, and Consciousness” (Xin Yi Shi Xiang Pin)
src.q: The scriptural source for [[alaya|ālaya-consciousness]] “following along with the body and holding it fast”, and for the statement “the mind-consciousness of all seeds”.
The argument establishing [[alaya|ālaya-consciousness]].
It establishes the [[eight_consciousnesses|eighth consciousness]] by ten scriptural and logical proofs, and discusses manas in detail.

tt.fix: Brought to completion in the *Cheng Weishi Lun* (659)
tt.trans: Tang: Xuanzang's translations of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* (647) and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (646–648); the *Cheng Weishi Lun* (659, Xuanzang’s composite translation of ten masters’ commentaries, recorded by Kuiji)

name: Ālaya-consciousness
desc:
The [[eight_consciousnesses|eighth consciousness]], which contains all seeds and becomes manifest when conditions obtain; it is the vehicle of the [[continuity|continuity]] of karma and of the continuation of life. “Ālaya” means “storehouse” and has three senses: the store (neng cang, that which can contain the seeds of all dharmas), the stored (suo cang, that which is perfumed by all dharmas and is their basis), and the storehouse of appropriation (zhi cang, that which is grasped as “I” by manas).

Its operation is described as “constantly turning like a violent torrent”: it arises and perishes moment by moment yet continues without interruption, neither permanent nor annihilated. This simile answers two errors at once: taking it as permanent (which would make it a substantial self), and taking it as annihilated (which would leave the fruits of karma without an owner).

The tathāgatagarbha tradition offers another reading: the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* (Ru Lengqie Jing), fascicle 7, says, “The ālaya-consciousness is called the tathāgatagarbha, and is together with the seven consciousnesses of ignorance” — this equates ālaya-consciousness with the tathāgatagarbha, bringing the “consciousness” of Yogācāra and the “mind-nature” of the tathāgatagarbha tradition into convergence in later Indian and Chinese Buddhist thought.

src.t: *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, “Chapter on the Marks of Mind, Manas, and Consciousness” (Xin Yi Shi Xiang Pin)
src.q: An account of the functions of “the mind-consciousness of all seeds” and “holding fast to the body”.
The three senses of “storehouse”; “constantly turning like a violent torrent”.
“The ālaya-consciousness is called the [[tathagatagarbha|tathāgatagarbha]], and is together with the seven consciousnesses of ignorance.”

tt.trans: Northern Wei: Bodhiruci and others' translation, *Ru Lengqie Jing* (513); Tang: Śikṣānanda's translation, *Mahāyāna Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* (700–704)

name: Transformation of Consciousness into Wisdom
desc:
The core of “transformation of the basis”: turning away from the defiled and turning toward the pure. “Transformation of consciousness into wisdom” means that the [[eight_consciousnesses|eight consciousnesses]] are transformed into the [[four_wisdoms|four wisdoms]]; it is the ultimate goal of Yogācāra.

In “transformation of the basis” (āśraya-parāvṛtti) the “basis” (āśraya) means that which is relied upon — ālaya-consciousness and all its seeds. Transformation of the basis does not mean that the substance of the mind changes, but that the “basis” of consciousness turns from defiled to pure: the eighth consciousness becomes the great mirror wisdom, the seventh becomes the wisdom of equality, the sixth becomes the wisdom of wondrous observation, and the first five become the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done.

The key lies in the word “transformation”: it is not the annihilation of consciousness and the creation of another wisdom, but the transformation of the same function once grasping has been relinquished. This is structurally akin to Madhyamaka's “afflictions are themselves enlightenment” and Tiantai's “a single moment of ignorance is the mind of the Dharma-nature”, though Yogācāra preserves a more detailed account of the stages and the mechanism.

src.q: The sequence and correlation by which the [[eight_consciousnesses|eight consciousnesses]] are transformed into the four wisdoms.
A systematic exposition of transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti).

name: The Four Wisdoms

src.q: The establishment and correlation of the [[four_wisdoms|four wisdoms]].
It explains the qualities of the stage of Buddhahood by way of the [[four_wisdoms|four wisdoms]].

name: Tathāgatagarbha
desc:
The basis for attaining Buddhahood that all sentient beings intrinsically possess; that is, [[pure_mind|the intrinsically pure mind]] and [[buddha_nature|Buddha-nature]], merely covered by ignorance and not yet manifest. The literal meaning of “tathāgatagarbha” (ru lai zang) is “the Tathāgata in the womb” — the Tathāgata is present in potency within the bodies of sentient beings.

It provides the ontological basis for attaining Buddhahood and explains the mechanism of delusion and awakening: the mind-nature is intrinsically pure, but is defiled by adventitious dust. Delusion and awakening are therefore not a difference between “having” and “not having” but between “covered” and “manifest”.

“Garbha” has three senses (*Buddha-nature Treatise*, Fo Xing Lun, fascicle 2, “Chapter on the Tathāgatagarbha”):
- the garbha as that which is encompassed: all sentient beings are encompassed within the wisdom of the Tathāgata;
- the garbha as concealment: the dharma-body does not change in either the causal or the fruition stage, yet sentient beings cannot see it because they are covered by affliction;
- the garbha as that which encompasses: the qualities of the Tathāgata's fruition are entirely encompassed within the minds of ordinary beings.

This page situates the concept in the line of inquiry concerned with the “basis for attaining Buddhahood” — namely: once non-self has been established, the subjective ground for Buddhahood can only fall on the mind-nature itself. This placement is not, however, the consensus of all schools: Prāsaṅgika Madhyamaka does not accept a truly existent tathāgatagarbha (for fear of falling into eternalism), nor does Yogācāra wholly equate its own position with the tathāgatagarbha; Chinese Tiantai, Huayan, and Chan, by contrast, absorbed it extensively and made it central to their doctrinal classification.

src.q: By nine similes — a transformed Buddha within a lotus, pure honey in a rock-tree, true gold fallen into an impure place, a golden image wrapped in worthless cloth, a lowly woman bearing a noble child, and so on — it explains that the Tathāgata is intrinsically present within the bodies of sentient beings. It is generally regarded as the earliest [[tathagatagarbha|tathāgatagarbha]] scripture to appear.

src.t: *Śrīmālādevī Sūtra* (Shengman Jing), “Chapter on the Dharma-body” (Fa Shen Zhang)
src.q: “The Tathāgata's dharma-body, not separate from the store of affliction, is called the [[tathagatagarbha|tathāgatagarbha]].” “The tathāgatagarbha enveloped by the store of immeasurable affliction.”
It uses gold in ore as a simile for the way the [[tathagatagarbha|tathāgatagarbha]] contains the pure dharma-body; all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature.
“The tathāgatagarbha is the cause of good and evil, and can bring forth all sentient beings universally.” “The ālaya-consciousness is called the [[tathagatagarbha|tathāgatagarbha]].”
The three senses of “garbha”: the garbha as that which is encompassed, the garbha as concealment, and the garbha as that which encompasses.

tt.form: c. 3rd–2nd century BCE (the first stirrings of the doctrine that the mind-nature is intrinsically pure; the preface chapter of the *Ekottara-āgama* (Zeng Yi Ahan Jing) already contains the phrase “the universally retaining tathāgatagarbha”, zong chi ru lai zang)
tt.fix: Between roughly the 3rd and 5th centuries a scriptural corpus centred on the *Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra*, the *Śrīmālādevī Sūtra*, the *Anūnatvāpūrṇatvanirdeśa* (Bu Zeng Bu Jian Jing), the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, and the *Ratnagotravibhāga* formed in India
tt.trans: *Da Fangdeng Rulai Zang Jing* (Buddhabhadra, Eastern Jin, early 5th century); *Shengman Jing* (Guṇabhadra, Liu Song, 436); *Da Ban Niepan Jing* (Dharmakṣema, Northern Liang, 421); *Ru Lengqie Jing* (Bodhiruci, Northern Wei, 513)

name: Buddha-nature
desc:
The possibility of awakening and the ultimate basis that sentient beings intrinsically possess. “Buddha-nature”, [[tathagatagarbha|tathāgatagarbha]], [[pure_mind|the intrinsically pure mind]], the dharma-nature, suchness, and the real mark are concepts that are “one in meaning though different in name”.

There is one important divergence between the Indian Buddhist doctrine of “lineage” (gotra) and the Chinese doctrine of “Buddha-nature”: Indian Yogācāra posits the “five lineages” (the śrāvaka lineage, the pratyekabuddha lineage, the bodhisattva lineage, the indeterminate lineage, and the lineage-less), maintaining that sentient beings of the “lineage-less” kind can never attain Buddhahood; whereas the position of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* that “all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature” became the basis for the consensus of Chinese Buddhist thought that “all can attain Buddhahood”.

This divergence has considerable practical consequences: if there are lineage-less sentient beings, then “universal salvation” has a theoretical limit; if all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature, then the scope of the bodhisattva path is infinite. Both Tiantai and Huayan adopt the latter.

src.q: “All sentient beings possess the [[buddha_nature|Buddha-nature]]”; it uses gold in ore as a simile.

src.t: *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna* (Da Cheng Qixin Lun)
src.q: It opens the “one mind” into the two gates of [[suchness|suchness]] and of arising-and-ceasing, and holds that sentient beings intrinsically possess the nature of enlightenment.
The doctrine of the five lineages, which stands opposed to the position that “all possess the [[buddha_nature|Buddha-nature]]”.

tt.fix: “All sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature” in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*; the Yogācāra doctrine of the five lineages runs parallel to it
tt.trans: Dharmakṣema's translation of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* under the Northern Liang (421) — thereby “all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature” became the settled conclusion of Chinese Buddhism

name: The Intrinsically Pure Mind
desc:
The mind-nature is intrinsically pure, but is defiled by adventitious dust. Delusion and awakening are therefore not the acquisition of something new, but the removal of a covering.

The thesis that “the mind-nature is intrinsically pure” (Pali pabhassara-citta) already appears in the Āgamas and the schools: the mind is defiled by adventitious dust and affliction, yet the nature of the mind is pure. The schools differed on this — the [[sarvastivada|Sarvāstivāda]] and others held that “the mind-nature is intrinsically pure” refers to “the possibility that the mind will attain Buddhahood in the future” rather than to “being pure right now”.

In the [[tathagatagarbha|tathāgatagarbha]] tradition, the *Śrīmālādevī Sūtra*'s “the intrinsically pure mind, defiled by adventitious dust and affliction” became the standard formulation. “Adventitious dust” combines two images, “adventitious” (a temporary guest, not a permanent resident) and “dust” (an external accretion). Adventitious dust is thus the imagined nature — what covers the mind-nature is grasping, not the mind-nature itself.

This structure makes practice a matter of “removing the covering” rather than “fabricating”: there is no need to produce a pure mind, only to remove the obscuration. Chan's “illuminating the mind and seeing one's nature” and Tiantai's “a single moment of ignorance is the mind of the Dharma-nature” both inherit this.

src.q: “The [[pure_mind|intrinsically pure mind]] is defiled by adventitious dust and affliction.”

name: The Bodhisattva Path
desc:
The core path of the Mahāyāna: arousing the mind of enlightenment, practising the [[six_paramitas|six pāramitās]], traversing the ten stages, and attaining Buddhahood in order to save sentient beings. It is the direction in which [[tathagatagarbha|tathāgatagarbha]] thought unfolds within Mahāyāna practice.

The key to the bodhisattva path lies in the “mind of enlightenment” (bodhicitta) — the aspiration to attain Buddhahood for the benefit of all sentient beings. This motive transforms practice from “seeking one's own liberation” into “liberation together with all sentient beings”, and on this ground the Mahāyāna criticises the śrāvaka vehicle as “self-serving”.

As to stages, the bodhisattva path comprises the ten stages (from the stage of Joy to the stage of the Dharma-cloud), coordinated with the ten pāramitās, and Buddhahood is attained after three great incalculable aeons. Huayan, Yogācāra, and Tiantai each have their own detailed assessment of the ten stages.

The point of connection between tathāgatagarbha thought and the bodhisattva path is this: since all sentient beings intrinsically possess the tathāgatagarbha, “saving sentient beings” is not the bestowal of something out of nothing but the helping of sentient beings to remove their covering and bring out what they intrinsically possess — this gives the bodhisattva path an inner necessity rather than making it a merely external command.

name: The Six Pāramitās
desc:
Giving, observance of precepts, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom. Also called the six pāramitās; “pāramitā” means “gone to the other shore” — by these six one can go from this shore of birth-and-death to the other shore of [[nirvana|nirvāṇa]].

The inner sequence of the six: giving first counteracts stinginess and greed; observance of precepts establishes a norm of conduct; patience keeps the first two unbroken in adverse circumstances; diligence keeps them uninterrupted; meditative concentration concentrates the power of the mind; wisdom keeps the first five from falling into grasping, so that they become “pāramitās” and not merely human and heavenly merit.

The treatises further speak of “cultivating the six pāramitās through three matters” — only when the six are combined with the three matters of “attention concomitant with the wisdom of omniscience, great compassion as the foremost, and non-acquisition as the expedient means” do they become the [[bodhisattva_path|bodhisattva path]] rather than mere virtuous action. This account makes the six pāramitās inseparable from the emptiness-wisdom of the Prajñāpāramitā.
